# Genetic and proteomic analysis identifies BAG3 as an amyloid‑responsive regulator of neuronal proteostasis

Zachary M. Augur1 · Garrett M. Fogo1 · Mason R. Arbery1 · Yi‑Chen Hsieh1 · Nalini R. Rao2 · Kritika Goyal2 · Emily Dexter2 · David A. Bennett3 · Jeffrey N. Savas2 · Andrew M. Stern1 · Tracy L. Young‑Pearse1

Received: 15 June 2025 / Revised: 26 September 2025 / Accepted: 2 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025

Abstract The autophagy–lysosome pathway (ALP) and the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) are the primary protein degradative mechanisms maintaining proteostasis in neurons. However, the impact of human genetic variation on these pathways and the role of BAG3 are poorly understood, particularly in the context of Alzheimer’s disease, where proteostatic dysfunction is a defining hallmark. We utilized a large panel of iPSCs from deeply phenotyped cohorts to interrogate genetic contributions to baseline autophagic flux and UPS activity in human neurons, and protein turnover was assessed using SILAC-based quantitative proteomics. Across this panel of neurons, we observed substantial inter-individual differences in autophagic flux, which was inversely correlated with UPS activity. This reciprocal relationship extended to tau homeostasis, where higher autophagic flux resulted in reduced accumulation of aggregated, phosphorylated tau. Proteomic analyses revealed that global protein turnover dynamics stratified based on degradation pathway activity and could predict pathway-specific substrate dependencies. Interestingly, Bcl-2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3), an important member of the chaperone-assisted selective autophagy pathway, emerged as a dynamically regulated autophagy chaperone, responsive to pharmacological inhibition of both the UPS and ALP. BAG3 knockout in neurons decreased autophagic flux and increased levels of high-molecular-weight phosphorylated tau. Notably, familial AD mutations and Aβ exposure induced BAG3 expression in neurons, while elevated BAG3 levels in human brain tissue were associated with higher neuropathological burden and disease progression. Our findings identify BAG3 as a key modulator of proteostasis in human neurons. Its regulation across genetic backgrounds and pathological stimuli suggests a central role in maintaining degradation activities in Alzheimer’s disease and related disorders.

## Introduction

The maintenance of protein homeostasis, or proteostasis, is critical for normal cell functioning and is largely governed by the coordinated actions of the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) and the autophagy–lysosome pathway (ALP) [22,

24]. Together, these pathways form the core of the protein quality control network, ensuring the removal of damaged, misfolded, or aggregated proteins, as well as dysfunctional organelles [72]. The UPS is responsible for the degradation of most proteins, but particularly soluble and ubiquitinated proteins [39, 72]. The narrow 20S core particle necessitates the unfolding of substrates prior to degradation, limiting the UPS to non-aggregated proteins [3, 87]. In contrast, the ALP mediates the breakdown of oligomeric or aggregated proteoforms and even entire organelles [6, 28, 50, 62]. Although mechanistically distinct, the ALP and UPS are highly interconnected components of the protein quality control system, with increasing evidence pointing to functional crosstalk between them [18, 36, 41, 96]. The degradation route for a given substrate depends on multiple factors, including substrate size, conformation, structure, and ubiquitin linkage, as well as the cellular context and stress

Ubiquitination is a shared post-translational modification relevant for targeting to both systems, and evidence suggests that polyubiquitin modified lysine residues may influence pathway selection [45, 59, 65]. Moreover, shared ubiquitin receptors such as p62/SQSTM1 act at the intersection of both systems, mediating substrate delivery to autophagosomes while also participating in feedback regulation of proteasomal function [69, 95]. In addition, components of each degradation system can be regulated by the other, providing further integration and homeostatic control. For example, proteasome subunits have been shown to be degraded by autophagy under certain stress conditions [21, 73]. One of the most striking examples of this functional crosstalk is the compensatory relationship that emerges when one degradation pathway is impaired. Upon UPS inhibition or overload, cells activate autophagy to help clear the resulting buildup of ubiquitinated or aggregated proteins [1, 53, 77]. Conversely, ALP impairment can alter proteasomal activity, which is particularly impactful for substrates that remain soluble enough to be handled by the UPS [43]. This reciprocal relationship reflects a fundamental adaptation within the protein quality control network to ensure cellular survival under proteotoxic conditions. Notably, this balance is often disrupted in neurodegenerative diseases. It is hypothesized that with age, protein degradation efficiency broadly declines [26, 73, 88]. This reduction in efficiency may be the result of an increased protein aggregation burden in aged or diseased cells where autophagy becomes increasingly critical in clearing protein aggregates [7, 33, 42, 64, 84, 86]. Despite the relevance of this compensatory relationship following stress or stimulation, we are unaware of any studies of basal protein degradation activity and global protein turnover performed across genetic backgrounds in human neurons. One important protein that may influence this protein degradation network crosstalk is Bcl2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3) [17, 27, 82]. BAG3 is a stress-induced chaperone protein that maintains protein quality control under conditions of proteotoxic stress via chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA) [54]. It has been shown that upon proteasome inhibition or saturation, BAG3 is significantly upregulated to compensate for reduced protein degradation capacity [33, 58, 60, 91, 98]. BAG3 is also thought to regulate tau homeostasis, as overexpression promotes tau clearance while knockdown leads to accumulation [23, 25, 52, 83, 85]. BAG3 interacts with autophagy receptors such as p62/SQSTM1 and cytoskeletal elements such as synaptopodin, facilitating the transport of tau aggregates to autophagosomes [35, 55]. Furthermore, BAG3 has been implicated in modulating endosomal pathways through the regulation of RAB35 activity, thereby influencing tau degradation via the endolysosomal system

[56]. Notably, BAG3 expression is variable among neuronal subtypes; excitatory neurons, which are more susceptible to tau pathology in Alzheimer’s disease, exhibit lower BAG3 levels compared to inhibitory neurons, suggesting a potential link between BAG3 expression and neuronal vulnerability to tau pathologies [25]. These findings underscore the multifaceted role of BAG3 in tau clearance and its potential as a therapeutic target. In this study, we used a panel of 47 human iPSC lines from the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) cohorts, ongoing longitudinal clinical–pathologic cohorts of aging and Alzheimer’s disease, to examine how genetic diversity influences protein degradation in human neurons [8]. By measuring both autophagic flux and UPS activity across lines, we found an inverse relationship between these two degradative pathways. We next studied global protein turnover to identify substrates preferentially degraded by each pathway, which revealed that turnover rates of specific proteins can serve as predictive markers of autophagy or UPS activity in neurons. Finally, we focused on the stress-responsive co-chaperone BAG3, which emerged as a key modulator of protein degradation in neurons. Our results identify BAG3 as an Aβ-responsive effector of protein degradation and tau clearance, underscoring its central role in the molecular pathophysiology of Alzheimer’s disease.

Participants enrolled without known dementia and agreed to annual clinical evaluation and brain donation. All signed informed and repository consents and an Anatomic Gift Act. CRISPR/Cas9 editing to generate BAG3 WT, HET, and KO iPSCs

The following lines were chosen for CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis of BAG3: BR33 and BR24, two iPSC lines derived from non-cognitively impaired individuals (male and female, respectively) from the ROSMAP cohorts [46]. gRNA ‘GCA​GCG​ATT​CCG​AAC​TGA​GG’ was used to target exon 2 within the BAG3 sequence, which is conserved within relevant BAG3 transcript isoforms. The Zhang Lab CRISPR Design website (crispr.mit.edu) was used to generate guide RNAs (gRNAs) with minimal off-target effects. gRNAs were cloned into the pXPR- 003 vector. hiPSCs were electroporated with the sgRNAencoding plasmid and Cas9, and cells were isolated for monoclonal selection and Sanger sequenced to determine BAG3 mutations. The cells were then replated at 200 k cells/cm2 using StemFlex Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and ROCK inhibitor (10 µM) (day 0). The media were changed to KSR media (day 1), 1:1 of KSR and N2B media (day 2), and N2B media (day 3). On day 4, cells were dissociated using accutase and plated at 50 k cells/cm2 using iN D4 media (NBM media + 1:50 B27 + BDNF, GDNF, CNTF (10 ng/mL, Peprotech). Doxycycline (2 μg/ml, Sigma) was added from day 1 to the end of the differentiation, and puromycin (5 µg/ml, Gibco) was added from day 2 to the end of the differentiation. On day 3, B27 supplement (1:100, Life Technologies) was added. From day 4 to the end of the

differentiation, cells were cultured in iN day 4 media and fed every 2–3 days [57]. Induced neuron protocol media:

AHA labeling and protein turnover measurements

On day 20 of iN cell culture, cells were switched to methionine starvation media (DMEM no methionine no cysteine (Gibco 21–013-024) with 1 × B27 supplement, 0.22 µM sodium pyruvate, 5 µg/mL NAC, 10 ng/mL CNTF, 10 ng/mL BDNF, 10 ng/mL GDNF, 2 µg/mL doxycycline) overnight at 37  °C. On day 21, starvation media was supplemented with 500 µM L-Azidohomoalanine (AHA; Vector Laboratories, CCT-1066) for 24 h to label newly synthesized proteins. After 24  h, iN media was fully changed to complete NBM after DPBS wash. AHA-labeled proteins were chased out in NBM for 7 days. The translation (100%) control for each genotype was lysed immediately after AHA 24-h incubation. Lysates were then prepared as normal for western blotting, as described above. To measure protein turnover, cell lysates were incubated with

5 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma, I6125) for 30 min at room temperature. Lysates were then incubated with 100 µM DBCO-PEG4-Biotin (Tocris, 7480) for 30 min at room temperature. Western blots were performed as described above. For the rabbit anti-Biotin antibody, it was used at a 1:2000 dilution. The amount of Biotin signal per sample was normalized to REVERT total protein stain and then the 100% translation control to yield the % of Biotin remaining, an indicator of protein turnover during the 7-day chase period.

Stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) using iNs

SILAC labeling

SILAC was employed to investigate protein dynamics during neuronal differentiation. Cells were cultured in media supplemented with heavy isotope-labeled amino acids (Lys + 8, CNLM29-H-1 and Arg + 10 CNLM539-H1 from Cambridge Isotopes) starting at day 14 of differentiation (designated D0 for SILAC labeling). The heavy-labeled media contained 15N. Following the onset of heavy isotope labeling (after D0 harvest), cells were harvested at various time points: D1, D2, D7, D14, and D21, corresponding to 1-, 2-, 7-, 14-, and 21-day post-labeling, respectively. Four distinct lines: BR26, BR57, BR58, and BR98 were used in parallel for all time points. Cell lysates from each line at every time point were prepared and subjected to quantitative mass spectrometry-based proteomic analysis to assess changes in protein expression and turnover during differentiation [89].

Mass spectrometry sample preparation

For the MS analysis, proteins from the cell lysate were precipitated using chloroform/methanol protein precipitation followed by denaturation, reduction, alkylation, enzymatic digestion, peptide cleanup, and high-pH reversed-phase fractionation. Methanol and chloroform were added in a 4:1:3 ratio (sample:methanol:chloroform), followed by vortexing and centrifugation at high speed to separate phases. The aqueous layer was discarded, and the protein pellet was washed with methanol and briefly air-dried. The pellet was then resuspended in 100 µL of 6 M guanidine hydrochloride and incubated at 95 °C for 10 min to ensure complete solubilization. Disulfide bonds were reduced by adding 0.5 µL of 1 M dithiothreitol (DTT), followed by incubation at 56 °C for 20 min. After cooling to room temperature, 3 µL of 500 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) was added to alkylate the reduced cysteine residues. Samples were incubated in the dark at room temperature for 20 min. Excess IAA was quenched by adding 5 µL of 1 M DTT and incubating for 15 min at room temperature. Then, samples

were digested with mass spectrometry grade trypsin/Lys-c mix (Promega, Cat# V5073) overnight at 37 °C. The reaction was subsequently stopped by acidification with 1% formic acid (FA) and desalted using HyperSep C18 Cartridges (Thermo Scientific, Cat# 60108-302) per manufacturer’s instructions. Eluates were dried using a vacuum concentrator and stored at − 80 °C. Dried peptides were reconstituted in 300 µL of 0.1% triethylamine (TEA) in water and fractionated using the Pierce™ High-pH Reversed-Phase Peptide Fractionation Kit (Thermo Scientific, Cat# 84868). Fractionation was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol, with stepwise elution using 5%, 10%, 15%, and 50% acetonitrile (ACN) in 0.1% TEA. Each of the four resulting fractions was collected, dried under vacuum, and stored at − 80 °C until LC–MS/MS analysis. Each dried high-pH fraction was further desalted using Pierce™ C18 Spin Columns (Thermo Scientific, Cat# 89852) to remove residual TEA and salts. Final eluates were dried using a vacuum concentrator and stored at − 80 °C until LC–MS/MS analysis [73].

Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS)

Dried peptide samples were resuspended in 20 µL of Buffer A (94.875% H₂O, 5% acetonitrile [ACN], and 0.125% formic acid [FA]). A total of 3 µg of peptide was injected via autosampler and loaded onto a PepMap™ 100 C18 nanoViper™ trap column (75 µm × 2 cm, Thermo Fisher Scientific) using an UltiMate™ 3000 HPLC system. Peptides were then separated on an analytical PepMap™ RSLC C18 column (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a stainless-steel emitter tip and analyzed using a Nanospray Flex™ ion source operating at 2,000 V. Chromatographic separation was performed over a 2.5-h gradient using Buffer A (94.875% H₂O, 5% ACN, 0.125% FA) and Buffer B (99.875% ACN, 0.125% FA). The elution gradient consisted of 2–8% Buffer B over 6 min, 8–24% over 64 min, 24–36% over 20 min, 36–55% over 10 min, 55–95% over 10 min, followed by 10 min at 95%, and finally re-equilibration to 2% Buffer B over 30 min. Peptides were analyzed on an Orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using data-dependent acquisition. MS1 survey scans were acquired in the Orbitrap at a resolution of 60,000, over a scan range of 300–1500 m/z. MS parameters were: ion transfer tube temperature, 300 °C; Easy-IC internal mass calibration; default charge state, 2; automatic gain control (AGC) target, 2 × ­105; maximum injection time, 50 ms; microscans, 1; and S-lens RF level, 60. Data were collected in positive ion mode with centroid format. MIPS was enabled. Charge states from 2 to 6 were selected for fragmentation; unassigned precursors were excluded. Dynamic

Mass spectrometry data analysis and quantification

Protein identification, quantification, and analysis were performed with Integrated Proteomics Pipeline—IP2 (Integrated Proteomics Applications, Inc., San Diego, CA. http://​www.​integ​rated​prote​omics.​com/) using ProLuCID, DTASelect2, Census, and QuantCompare. Spectrum raw files were extracted into MS1, MS2 files using RawExtract 1.9.9 (http://​fields.​scrip​ps.​edu/​downl​oads.​php). The tandem mass spectra were searched against the UniProt human protein database (downloaded on 06-03-2022), matched to sequences using the ProLuCID/SEQUEST algorithm (ProLuCID version 3.1) with 20 ppm peptide mass tolerance for precursor ions and 600 ppm for fragment ions. ProLuCID searches included all fully and half-tryptic peptide candidates that fell within the mass tolerance window and had no miscleavages. Carbamidomethylation (+ 57.02146 Da) of cysteine was considered as a static modification. Peptide/spectrum matches (PSMs) were assessed in DTASelect2 using the cross-correlation score (XCorr) and normalized difference in cross-correlation scores (DeltaCN). Peptide probabilities and false-discovery rates (FDR) were calculated based on a target/decoy database containing the reversed sequences of all the proteins appended to the target. For each brain region per biological replicates, proteins identified had an FDR of ≤ 1% at the protein level. Each protein identified was required to have a minimum of one peptide of minimal length of six amino acid residues. For the SILAC experiments, each dataset was searched twice, once against light (14N) and then against heavy (8.0142 K and 10.0083 R) protein databases. After the results from ProLuCID were filtered using DTASelect2, ion chromatograms were generated using “Census”. Census allows users to filter peptide ratio measurements based on a correlation threshold because the correlation coefficient (values between zero and one) represents the quality of the correlation between the unlabeled and labeled chromatograms and can be used to filter out poor quality measurements. This correlation coefficient also considers

the retention time of the identified spectra. Peptide ratio measurements used for further analysis exceeded a profile score of 0.8. Fractional abundance was calculated from the “light” and “heavy” peptide chromatograms, and for each respective protein, the 14N and 15N chromatograms for the respective peptides were averaged. The protein remaining was then calculated from those “light” and “heavy” averages to finally compare across DIVs. Final protein ratios were generated with QuantCompare, which uses Log twofold change on the biological replicates. The statistical significance of the differential expression for all proteins was assessed using a two-tailed one-sample Student’s t-test on their corresponding peptide quantification ratios between both conditions. The obtained p values were FDR-adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Proteins with FDRadjusted p values < 0.05 and measured in at least two biological replicates in both conditions were considered for further analyses [89]. The percentage of “light” protein remaining at an individual harvest day was calculated by dividing the light/heavy ratio at the day of interest by the corresponding value at harvest D1. Proteins that displayed light/heavy ratios > 1 were excluded from analysis. Proteins measured in all four genetic backgrounds in at least 2 differentiations at harvest D7 and D14 were used for principal component analysis (PCA). PCA was performed in R studio using the factoextra library. Dimension coordinates for individual lines and proteins were exported and visualized in GraphPad Prism 10.

Tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling

Peptides were reconstituted in 100 μl of 100 mM triethyl ammonium bicarbonate (TEAB), and labeling was performed using TMTPro isobaric tags (Thermofisher Scientific, A44520) as previously described [31, 70]. Briefly, the TMT labeling reagents were equilibrated to room temperature, and anhydrous ACN (200 mL) was added to each reagent channel. Each channel was gently vortexed for 5 min, and then 20 mL from each TMT channel was transferred to the peptide solutions and allowed to incubate for 1 h at room temperature. The reaction was quenched with 5% (v/v) hydroxylamine (5 mL) (Pierce). All 16 channels were then combined and dried by SpeedVac (LabConco) to approximately 100 mL and diluted with 1 mL of 0.1% (v/v) TFA, then acidified to a final concentration of 1% (v/v) FA and 0.1% (v/v) TFA. Peptides were desalted with a 60 mg HLB plate (Waters). The eluates were then dried to completeness. High-pH fractionation was performed essentially as described with slight modification [71]. Dried samples were resuspended in high-pH loading buffer (0.07% v/v NH4OH, 0.045% v/v FA, 2% v/v ACN) and loaded onto a Water’s BEH (2.1 x 150 mm with 1.7 µm beads). A Thermo Vanquish UPLC system was used to carry out the fractionation. Solvent A consisted of 0.0175% (v/v) ­NH4OH, 0.01125% (v/v) FA, and 2% (v/v) ACN; solvent B consisted of 0.0175% (v/v) ­NH4OH, 0.01125% (v/v) FA, and 90% (v/v) ACN. The sample elution was performed over a 25 min gradient with a flow rate of 0.6 mL/min with a gradient from 0 to 50% B. A total of 96 individual equal volume fractions were collected across the gradient and dried to completeness using vacuum centrifugation.

Data processing protocol

All raw files were searched using Thermo’s Proteome Discoverer suite (version 2.4.1.15) with Sequest HT. The spectra were searched against a human Uniprot database downloaded August 2020 (86,395 target sequences). Search parameters included a 10 ppm precursor mass window, a

0.05 Da product mass window, dynamic modifications for methionine (+ 15.995 Da), deamidated asparagine and glutamine (+ 0.984 Da), phosphorylated serine, threonine, and tyrosine (+ 79.966 Da), and static modifications for carbamidomethyl cysteines (+ 57.021 Da) and N-terminal and Lysine-tagged TMT (+ 304.207 Da). Percolator was used to filter PSMs to 0.1%. Peptides were grouped using strict parsimony, and only razor and unique peptides were used for protein level quantitation. Reporter ions were quantified from MS2 scans using an integration tolerance of 20 ppm with the most confident centroid setting. Abundance data were ­log2 transformed, and batch effects were regressed using ComBat [51]. Differential expression was calculated using the DEP package in R [100].

## Results

Genetically encoded variation in autophagic activity demonstrates balance with UPS activity and influence on tau degradation

The autophagy–lysosome pathway (ALP) and the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS) are the two primary mechanisms by which cells maintain proteostasis, each responsible for degrading misfolded, damaged, or excess proteins. These systems are hypothesized to exhibit some level of compensation, such that inhibition or dysfunction in one may lead to upregulation of the other (Fig. 1a) [1, 43, 53, 77]. However, the way in which human genetic variability shapes basal protein degradation activity, particularly in post-mitotic neurons, remains understudied. To address this, we assessed autophagic flux (AF) across iPSC-derived neurons (iNs) derived from 47 participants in the ROSMAP cohorts which include individuals with diagnosed Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and age- and sexmatched individuals who were not cognitively impaired (NCI) (Fig. 1b, c, Supplemental Table 1, 2). AF was measured by quantifying the accumulation of LC3B-II, a marker of autophagosomes, following treatment with the autophagy inhibitor chloroquine. AF was inversely correlated with previously measured and reported proteasome activity in the same neuronal lines (Fig. 1d) [33]. This finding suggests baseline level balance and differences in the relative utilization of these two degradation systems in human neurons across genetic backgrounds. We previously identified associations between UPS activity and the level of tau, total ubiquitinated protein, and levels of the proteasome subunit PSMB5 in this same iN cohort [33]. Here, we found that AF is significantly associated with specific tau proteoforms and inversely associated with UPS activity, providing additional evidence of a reciprocal relationship between AF and UPS activity across the proteins measured (Fig. 1e). We then validated this analysis in a focused subset of iNs, where we again measured AF alongside total and phosphorylated tau species in the same lysates. Replicating our previous analyses, now in these paired lysates, we see that higher AF is positively associated with levels of total tau and significantly associated with monomeric phospho-tau proteoforms (Fig. 1f, g). In contrast, aggregated forms of phospho-tau (high-molecular-weight tau, HMW) exhibited a negative correlation with AF (Fig. 1h).

Basal protein degradation activity predicts neuronal global protein turnover signatures

We next aimed to study how differences in protein degradation activity influence global neuronal protein turnover. We therefore assayed protein turnover using continuous metabolic stable isotope labeling of amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) coupled with mass spectrometry-based proteomic analysis. Neurons from four individuals (highlighted with colored dots in Fig. 1d) with varying degradation capacities (high/low UPS and high/low AF) were cultured with media containing heavy isotope-labeled Arg and Lys amino acids starting at day 14 of differentiation (D14) and were harvested after 1, 2, 7, 14, or 21 days of labeling (Fig. 2a, Supplemental Table 3). Most proteins synthesized prior to heavy isotope labeling (termed “light” proteins) should demonstrate exponential decay over time due to protein degradation. The abundance of light protein remaining over time generally displayed patterns consistent with exponential decay in iNs from all four lines (Fig. 2b). Global protein turnover rates differed between neurons with high versus low UPS at D7 (of heavy labeling) (Fig. 2c); however, a global difference was not detected between neurons with high versus low AF (Fig. 2d). To determine if differences in protein degradation activities could be resolved by SILAC, we used principal component analysis (PCA) to examine patterns of individual protein degradation. Here, the median “percent light protein remaining” values at D7 and D14 (of heavy labeling) for neurons from each line were input as variables in the PCA (1,619 variables) to spatially separate individuals (Fig. 2e). In PCA space, lines separated strikingly similarly to the balance of UPS and AF activity (Fig. 1d), with dimension 1 mirroring UPS activity and dimension 2 mirroring differences in AF. Since global turnover on average was reduced in low versus high UPS lines (Fig. 2c) and the turnover rates of individual proteins were used as inputs to the PCA analysis, we predicted that the top contributing variables to dimension 1 could represent substrates of the UPS. To test this hypothesis, we identified proteins contributing strongly to dimension 1 that were consistent at D7 and D14 (Fig. 2f). For example, the actin-related protein CAPZA1 demonstrated a high contribution to dimension 1 and displayed faster turnover in neurons with the highest UPS, BR98 (Fig. 2g, Supplemental Fig. 1a). To test the dependence of protein turnover on the UPS, neurons were treated with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) for 48 h. Since the cultures are predominantly nondividing post-mitotic cells, the inhibition of protein synthesis makes protein abundance dependent on protein degradation alone. BAG3 modifies the autophagy–lysosome pathway and aggregated tau in neurons

To further examine the relationship between autophagy and UPS activity in human neurons, we compared proteomic profiles of iNs treated with either bortezomib or chloroquine (an autophagy inhibitor). The bortezomib treatment data were previously published [33], while the chloroquine dataset was newly generated for this study but performed in the same iN genetic background (Fig. 3a, Supplemental Table 4). By comparing differentially abundant proteins across both conditions, we identified a set of proteins that were inversely altered in response to perturbation of each degradation pathway (Fig. 3b). BAG3 (Bcl2-associated athanogene 3) exhibited one of the most substantial changes in relative protein level following either drug treatment, being upregulated by UPS inhibition and downregulated by autophagy inhibition (Fig. 3b). ZFAND5 and BNIP3 followed the same pattern, and both are linked to proteostasis [48, 99]. We then used the chloroquine and bortezomib proteomic profiles to generate gene set variation analysis (GSVA) enrichment scores [46]. When applied to BAG3 protein abundance across ROSMAP iNs, these scores revealed a positive correlation with bortezomib and a negative correlation with chloroquine, again highlighting the inverse relationship between these pathways and BAG3 (Supplemental Fig. 2a, b). We then validated the consistent BAG3 upregulation following bortezomib

treatment across iNs from eight additional genetic backgrounds from individuals with and without Alzheimer’s disease (AD) via western blot (Fig. 3c, d). We next asked whether loss of BAG3 would causally result in altered proteostasis. We generated BAG3 wildtype (WT) and knockout (KO) iPSC-derived iNs using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing in two genetic backgrounds (one male and one female ROSMAP participant; Supplemental Fig. 2c). Western blot analysis confirmed near-complete loss of BAG3 protein in KO iNs (Fig. 3e). AF was reduced in BAG3 KO iNs compared to WT (Fig. 3e, f). In contrast, a limited non-significant change in proteasome activity was observed in BAG3 KO iNs (Fig. 3g). Considering this, we assayed total ubiquitinated protein and global protein turnover with azidohomoalanine labeling (AHA labeling). In both cases, neither were altered with loss of BAG3 (Supplemental Fig. 3). We therefore investigated whether BAG3 KO specifically influenced the abundance of aggregation-prone proteins relevant in AD. BAG3 KO iNs exhibited a modest increase in high-molecular-weight (HMW) aggregated ­pTau214, while levels of total tau, and HMW and major ­pTau202/205, ­pTau181, and ­pTau217 remained unchanged (Fig. 3h–j, Supplemental Fig. 4a–f). This was largely in concordance with the findings observed in Fig. 1e. No significant changes were detected in Aβ or α-synuclein levels upon BAG3 KO (Supplemental Fig. 4g–i). Thus, BAG3 loss does not have a strong effect on levels of these aggregation-prone proteins in the absence of a stress-related stimulus.

Previous studies have proposed a compensatory relationship between autophagy and the UPS  under conditions of stress or experimental manipulation [1, 43, 53, 77]. However, to our knowledge, no prior work has systematically examined this interplay across genetically diverse human cell lines, let alone in neurons, under basal conditions. Our study is the first to reveal an inverse relationship between autophagic flux and UPS activity at baseline conditions, which is driven by lines with high/ low AF or UPS activity. This suggests that individual genetic variability can shape the intrinsic balance between autophagy and UPS activity, even in the absence of external stressors within neurons. Further studies are needed to identify and characterize the genetic determinants underlying these basal differences in degradative activity as they could have significant implications for the design of targeted therapies for neurodegenerative disease and beyond.

Another surprising yet important finding that reinforces the inverse relationship between AF and UPS activity is that global protein turnover profiles accurately predict the activity of these degradative pathways. Specifically, the turnover rates of substrates such as CFL1 and CAPZA1 serve as functional readouts of the underlying degradative capacity within neurons across genetic backgrounds. Interestingly, the proteins CFL1 and CAPZA1 lack canonical chaperonemediated autophagy KFERQ motifs (CAPZA1 includes only an acetylation-activated motif KEFIK), potentially contributing to preferential degradation by the UPS [40]. Investigating the degradation dynamics of proteins relevant to AD pathogenesis may therefore provide mechanistic insight into how the balance between autophagy and UPS influences disease progression [30]. Our findings with tau offer a clear example: baseline differences in autophagic and proteasomal activity predict pTau abundance, highlighting how disruptions in this balance may underlie tau accumulation and aggregation in disease. However, the distinct pTau proteoform change observed in our BAG3 KO iNs potentially reinforces the hypothesis that specific phosphorylated tau species are differentially targeted for degradation by the UPS or autophagy. These differences may reflect intrinsic selectivity of the cellular clearance mechanisms, differential accessibility of pTau proteoforms due to conformational or post-translational modifications, or could be influenced by the progression or severity of neurodegenerative disease states [2, 19, 47, 93]. While previous studies have shown that BAG3-mediated autophagy is robustly activated in response to proteasome inhibition [33, 58, 60, 91, 98], this phenomenon has not been thoroughly validated across human neurons of different genetic backgrounds and in a discovery-based proteomewide manner in neurons. Our work addresses this gap by applying highly sensitive quantitative proteomics to examine neuronal response to proteasome and autophagy inhibition. We identified BAG3 as one of the most strongly upregulated proteins in human neurons following proteasome inhibition, in line with its established role in promoting compensatory autophagy [33, 58, 60, 91, 98]. Previous studies have suggested that the balance between BAG1 and BAG3 is a key determinant of proteostasis, with BAG1 directing clients to the proteasome and BAG3 rerouting them to autophagy under conditions of proteasomal impairment or overload [63]. While BAG1 protein abundance does not increase in response to BAG3 ablation in these iNs [5], it remains possible that in the context of other relevant cellular stressors, an altered ratio of BAG1 to BAG3 may influence protein degradation and cellular proteostasis. Unexpectedly, BAG3 also was among the most significantly downregulated proteins upon autophagy inhibition with chloroquine. BAG3 may therefore be a critical regulatory node in maintaining balanced cellular autophagy and UPS activity, and additional studies are warranted to further explore this possibility. Leveraging this iPSC-derived neuronal system, we found that fAD mutations that increased Aβ production also upregulate BAG3, as did neurons treated with human AD brain extract in an Aβ-dependent manner [57]. Our global RNAseq analysis of these treated neurons revealed that BAG3 was not only one of the most significantly upregulated proteins following exposure to Aβ-containing extract but also defined a larger, coordinated network of stress-responsive proteins. Multiple components of the chaperone-assisted selective autophagy pathway and the heat shock response, such as HSPB8 and DNAJB1, also were co-upregulated. This points to an orchestrated proteostatic response, rather than an isolated BAG3 induction. We identified transcriptional regulators that were upregulated alongside BAG3 in response to Aβ, including BHLHE40, a transcription factor not previously linked to BAG3 or Aβ responses in neurons, but is best known for modulating circadian rhythms [14, 38, 67]. Additional studies may determine the transcriptional level control

of BAG3 in response to Aβ and whether BHLHE40 and circadian rhythm-related pathways could be implicated in its regulation, as has been suggested previously in astrocytes [80]. Lastly, we found that BAG3 protein is more abundant in AD brain than in control. Mirroring our observations in iNs, BAG3 levels correlate with disease severity and show correlations with cognitive decline, Braak stage, and pathological burden. These post-mortem findings further support our hypothesis that BAG3 upregulation may reflect a neuronal response to Aβ and point to a potential compensatory role for BAG3 in the human brain. This is consistent with previous studies demonstrating that rewiring of proteostatic systems, particularly the cellular chaperone network (chaperome), helps manage an increasingly insoluble proteome during differentiation and in pathologies such as AD. Specifically, it has been shown that aging attenuates chaperonin proteostasis, likely contributing to proteinopathies [90]. Another study showed that a subset of the chaperome is critical to maintaining proteostasis in aging and that changes in expression of the sub-network may signify early events leading to ageassociated proteostasis collapse with implications for the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disease [15]. A final study profiled the extent of chaperome deregulation in a panel of human cancers and neurodegenerative disorders and showed the importance of this chaperome network in regulating the proteostasis network in health and disease [15, 29, 90]. Although BAG3 is expressed in multiple brain cell types, our neuron-focused data suggest that neurons contribute, at least in part, to the diseaseassociated BAG3 signal. Future studies are warranted to determine how BAG3 regulation varies across cell types and whether similar proteostatic mechanisms are engaged in non-neuronal populations. In particular, the role of BAG3 in astrocytes remains poorly understood, and our group recently executed a study regarding the consequences of BAG3 reduction on astrocyte proteostasis [5]. Understanding this cellular specificity will be critical for evaluating the potential for BAG3 as a therapeutic target in AD.

## Conclusions

Taken together, our findings point toward a role for BAG3 in neuronal proteostasis and proteotoxic stress response. More specifically, the loss of BAG3 in neurons leads to a marked reduction in autophagic activity and a concomitant increase in aggregated pTau, implicating BAG3 in proteostasis.
